questions.enonce_markdown: Evaluate the importance of giving ancestral names to new born babies in African Traditional Religions. (25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In many African societies a child is given a name soon after birth during a naming ceremony, and the name may be that of an ancestor or a relative who has died. These are generalities, and customs differ from one people to another. The practice has religious, social and cultural importance.

**1. Belief in the continuity of life.** In ATR, death is not the end but a passage to the world of the ancestors, who are called the "living-dead" by Mbiti. Giving an ancestral name expresses the belief that the ancestor is remembered and in some societies that his or her spirit or character returns in the child. Names such as the Yoruba Babatunde ("father has returned") and Yetunde ("mother has returned") express this idea. Not all peoples understand this as literal rebirth: for some it is a way of honouring and linking the child to the ancestor.

**2. Link between the living and the dead.** The ancestors are guardians of the family and the community. A child named after one is placed under his or her protection and blessing. The living keep their memory by pronouncing the name, and by doing so the ancestors remain part of the family.

**3. Identity and belonging.** The name tells the child's family, lineage, clan and sometimes the circumstances of birth. It integrates the child into the community, which is more important than the individual in African thought ("I am because we are").

**4. Religious ceremonies.** The naming ceremony involves prayers, libations, the pouring of water, and sometimes sacrifices, in which the elders and the family call on the Supreme Being and the ancestors to bless, protect and guide the child. The child is thereby introduced into the religious life of the family.

**5. Moral and spiritual influence.** A name is believed to affect the character and destiny of the child. A child named after an ancestor is expected to take on the virtues of that person, and is taught to live in a way worthy of the name. The name also expresses hopes and gratitude to God.

**6. Continuity of the lineage.** Passing the names of the grandparents or great-grandparents down the generations keeps the family history alive and preserves oral tradition.

**7. Evaluation.** The practice remains important for maintaining family unity and cultural identity, and it has been adapted in Christian and Muslim families, who often give a baptismal or Islamic name as well as a family name. Its limits are that not all communities hold belief in the return of ancestors, some names may be given for the circumstances (twins, day of birth, a hard pregnancy), and a child is also seen as an individual in the community.

**Conclusion.** Giving ancestral names to newborn babies is important in ATR because it expresses belief in the continuity of life, links the child to the ancestors, gives identity and protection, and joins the child to the community. It remains a key part of African culture.
